messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] GMRFLib: Fail to factorize Q
messages.body_plain:
Yes, try the "cutoff" option for mesh=inla.mesh.create(loc,...).

Setting, for example, cutoff=4 only allows the triangulation algorithm to use input locations at an euclidean distance greater than 4.
The indices in
mesh$idx$loc
are then assigned, for each input point in  loc, the closest vertex in the resulting mesh.

In your case, this will smooth the boundary of the mesh.  From your picture, it looks as your'e using boundary=..., which can result in some of the interior "loc" points falling outside the resulting smoothed region.  That will not handled handled correctly by mesh$idx$loc, but apparently you don't have any "loc" input points so this may not be a problem, depending on how you use the resulting mesh later in the analysis.  Can't say anything more specific without the actual code.

/Finn

messages.subject_clean: spatial model from spBayes
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've been looking at the spBayes package recently, which implements some
nice spatial GLMM methods described here:

Banerjee et al 2008 Gaussian predictive process models for large spatial
data sets J. R. Statist. Soc. B, 70: 825ï¿½848

In this paper they specifically mention the possibility of implementing
their 'predictive process model' using inla (though before the R package
was developed), and I'm wondering if anyone has now done it? It would be
fantastic to fit this sort of model even more efficiently. My guess is
that writing this model for inla is far from trivial (and probably well
beyond my skills!), but if it can be done it would be even more
marvelous to extend it, if possible, to include an observation process
and be able to fit spatially explicit occupancy models.

So, if anyone knows if it's already done, if it's even feasible, and has
an idea of how much programming it woudl take I'd be interested to know.

Thanks!

C

--

Dr Colin Beale
Research Fellow
University of York

Mob. +255 (0) 684 059 123

Not at all! Thanks very much for sending these things, I've been working my way through them all adn think I understand what's going on. In summary for anyone else who reads along later, you've implemented the method (together with the authors) in INLA, but using Matlab code and it's not available in the r-inla package. On the other hand, I've missed the development of the SPDE approach, and as this is already implemented in r-inla I can see why you're not in any hurry to do the other method - from what I can see of the various implementations there are very few problems that Banerjee et al's method can come with that SPDE can't (perhaps slightly more flexible wrt covariance structure, but SPDE has Matern (which covers exponential), so no real shortage of options. It all looks very clever to me. So the final question is how easy would it be to extend the SPDE model to allow for an observation process to fit an occupancy model? In fact, my specific example is simpler than most occupancy models, as the observation process is simply an index of total effort to which I want to fit some decellerating function to estimate probability of detection given presence. (More than!) happy to discuss the more off-line if you're interested...

Thanks very much again - a great help!

Colin

data$A = as.numeric(data$A)

data$C = as.factor(data$C)
data$D = as.factor(data$D)

formula = y ~ 1 + A + B:A + C:A + D:A

## small test-example

y = 1:100

formula = y ~ 1 + B:A

On Sat, 2011-07-23 at 11:25 -0700, inti pedroso wrote:
> Thanks very much for that. I am sorry my notation was misleading. I
> should have spotted it. I have attached the model with corrected
> indexes and variables names.
> Your answer explains my current doubt. However, I still do not know
> how to code a second level of the regression, i.e., predictors for the
> J intercepts. I have noted better this model in the attached file.
> Sorry for wasting your time with little mistakes.

Here is your model. If the precision for the \alpha_j's are unknown, set
that correponding fixed to FALSE (or replace that statement with
f(A,model="iid"))

Best
H
**************

library(INLA)

load("example_data.RData")
data=z
rm(z)

data$A = as.factor(data$A)

mu.alpha = 0
prec.alpha = 0.001
mu.gamma = 0
prec.gamma = 0.0001
## need this as an offset since model="iid" has mean zero.
data$mu.alpha = rep(...,  dim(data)[1])

## set fixed = FALSE if the variance of \alpha_j is unknown.
formula = Y ~ -1 + offset(mu.alpha) +
    f(A, model="iid", initial = log(prec.alpha), fixed = TRUE) +

    B + C + D

r = inla(formula,  data = data,  family = "gaussian",
        control.fixed = list(mean = mu.gamma,  prec = prec.gamma))

messages.body_plain:
On Sat, 2011-07-30 at 04:14 -0700, Shige Song wrote:
> I am trying to estimate a simple logit (event ~ time) model in which
> there are may be 3-4 break points in time. I was wondering whether
> INLA can be used to automatically identify these break points and
> estimate their slopes. Thanks.
>
> Shige

Hi

inla itself cannot estimate changepoint models. however, you can
condition on the changepoint(s) and let inla calculate the marginal
likelihood. the attached example is simple, its just iid normals with
one changepoint in the mean level. by just trying out `all'
changepoinits, you get the posterior marginal for the changpoint (under
a uniform prior for the changepoints).

[ I added some extra stuff in the code so it will run faster ]

this can be explored further, and I point you to the report (to appear
in Bayesian Analysis);

http://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/r-inla.org/papers/changepoint-revised.pdf

hope this helps.

H
